title: First Redundant Link
statement: A telecom crew connects stations numbered 0 to stations - 1 by laying cables one at a time, in the order given by links, where each link [a, b] joins stations a and b. A link is redundant when the two stations it joins were already connected, directly or through other stations, before it was laid. Return the first redundant link as [a, b] exactly as it appears in links, or an empty array if no link is redundant. A link from a station to itself is redundant.

examples.explanation: After 0–1 and 1–2, stations 2 and 0 are already connected through 1, so [2, 0] is redundant.
Both links connect new pairs of stations.

hints.content: A link is redundant exactly when its endpoints already share a connected group.
You could answer that with a graph search over the links laid so far, but the groups change as links are laid.
Maintain a representative for each group; two stations are connected when they share a representative.
Merging two groups means pointing one representative at the other.
Path compression keeps representative lookups nearly constant as groups grow.

testCases.explanation: After 0–1 and 1–2, stations 2 and 0 are already connected through 1, so [2, 0] is redundant.
Both links connect new pairs of stations.
The second link repeats the first in reverse; it is returned as written.
The first four links build one chain; [4, 0] then closes a loop.
[3, 0] closes the loop 0–1–2–3 before [5, 4] repeats a link.
A star has no redundant link.

solutions.title: Search the earlier links before each new one
solutions.intuition: Before laying a link, check whether its endpoints are already connected by walking the network built so far.
solutions.approach: Keep adjacency lists of laid links. For each new link, depth-first search from one endpoint over the existing links; if the other endpoint is reached, the link is redundant. Otherwise add the link.
solutions.pseudocode: for each link (a, b): search from a over laid links; if b reached return [a, b]; add link; return [].
commonMistakes: Adding the link before searching, which makes every link look redundant.
Forgetting that a self-link means a and b are trivially the same station.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Rerunning a graph search before every link is correct but repeats work that grows with the network. A disjoint-set structure answers 'already connected?' and merges groups in near-constant amortized time, so the whole scan is nearly linear.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For links [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[2,3]], the searches before [0,1] and [1,2] find nothing.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Before [2,0], a search from 2 reaches 1 and then 0, so [2, 0] is returned.

solutions.title: Disjoint-set union with path compression
solutions.intuition: Connectivity only ever grows, so each station can point toward a representative of its group, and two stations are connected exactly when they share a representative.
solutions.approach: Start with every station as its own representative. For each link, find both representatives; if they match the link is redundant, otherwise merge by pointing one representative at the other. Path halving during find keeps the trees flat.
solutions.pseudocode: parent[i] = i; for each (a, b): ra = find(a), rb = find(b); if ra == rb return [a, b]; parent[ra] = rb; return [].
commonMistakes: Comparing parent[a] with parent[b] directly instead of their roots.
Returning the normalized pair [min, max] instead of the link as written.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I use union-find: each station points toward a group representative, find follows those pointers while halving the path, and union links one root under the other. A link whose endpoints already share a root closes a cycle, which is the redundancy we are asked for. With path compression the amortized cost per operation is inverse-Ackermann, so the scan is effectively linear.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For links [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[2,3]], link 0–1 merges 0 into 1's group and link 1–2 merges into 2's group.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: For link 2–0, find(2) and find(0) both return 2, so [2, 0] is returned before 2–3 is considered.
